children: India's official monthly gold imports have declined sharply since May 2026, but the fall could have both positive and negative implications, according to Kotak Institutional Equities.

The brokerage said the decline may reflect "(1) lower structural gold purchases by households deterred by higher gold import duties from May 13, 2026, (2) a temporary pause in gold purchases by households fearing import duty normalization (cut) or (3) increase in unofficial gold imports given higher domestic gold prices relative to global prices."

"Lower gold imports are a positive for India's CAD and BoP but may have 'hidden' negatives," Kotak said. It remains to be seen whether the decline represents "(1) a 'permanent' reset to lower household demand, (2) a temporary pause in gold purchase by households or (3) diversion of gold imports to unofficial channels with its negative repercussions for government taxes."
Good: Permanent reset in household demand
Kotak said higher import duties from May 13 may have reduced demand, with the increase resulting in a 9% rise in domestic gold prices relative to global gold prices.

Stable global and domestic gold prices may also have reduced gold's investment appeal, it said. The brokerage pointed to gold ETF flows as "a good indicator of household behavior linked to trailing returns of an asset class", noting a sharp rise in inflows in the second half of 2025 as gold prices increased and a sharp drop since February 2026 as prices declined.
Bad: Temporary pause in household demand

The decline "may simply reflect a temporary slowdown in gold purchases by Indian households" as they digest the one-time increase in domestic gold prices following higher duties and fear a duty cut could result in losses on recently purchased gold.
"Gold imports may recover to 'normal' levels if the government was to cut import duties," Kotak said, noting similar lulls and jumps following duty changes in the past.

The decline could also reflect "diversion of gold imports to unofficial channels and gold purchases by households from the unorganized sector", Kotak said, meaning official data could materially understate actual imports.
This could hurt government revenues through lower customs and GST collections if gold imports and purchases bypass official channels.

Kotak reiterated its long-standing view for higher GST rates and lower import duties on gold as an alternative route to "(1) reduce gold imports, (2) increase household gold recycling and (3) protect government revenues."

title: India's gold imports plunge, but is it good news? Kotak flags 3 scenarios
